artifacts.notes: The whole dictionary, A to Z. The retrieving lane searched it for "inner man" and found nothing, which is one of the four bounded negatives behind its finding that the gastric sense is a standing register rather than a novelist's coinage. 4268 LF-terminated lines, one per source paragraph. It is a transcription and not a facsimile: the printing's pagination, line breaks and typography are not recoverable from it.
artifacts.rights_basis: The work was first published in London in 1811, before 1929, so it is in the United States public domain by publication date. The Project Gutenberg wrapper -- its licence, its trademark references and its marker lines -- is excluded from this file by the stated transformation, so nothing Project Gutenberg authored survives in these bytes and Triptych claims no exclusive right in the source wording. THE FILE ITSELF NAMES NO PRINTING: its Project Gutenberg header gives only a title, an author, a translator or editor where there is one, a release date and a language, so the first-publication fact above is the work's, carried on this work's own record, and not a statement about which printing was transcribed. That is enough to settle the rights question and not enough to identify an edition, which is why the edition record claims none.

artifacts.rights_basis: Two things have to be separated. Project Gutenberg's permission page states that the vast majority of its eBooks are in the public domain in the United States and that nobody can grant or withhold permission to use them -- but that is a statement about the book, not about the file. This file is wrapped in Project Gutenberg's licence header and footer, which carry the Project Gutenberg trademark and conditions on its use. The wrapper-bearing bytes are therefore recorded as the hashed derivation input and are not retained in Git; what is retained is the derivative named in `notes`, from which the wrapper has been removed, leaving only the text whose rights the permission page settles.
